HELIX ENGINEERING & INTEGRATION | ALMAGEST DIVISION

HEI CORPORATE CANON SERIES

H-E-I — HELIX ENGINEERING & INTEGRATION

FULL CANONICAL COMPANY LORE

CURRENT MASTER VERSION

The master history of Helix Engineering & Integration - from its pre-Almagest engineering programs through the modern fleet, infrastructure, personnel, equipment, and frontier design philosophy.

HEI became indispensable not by building the biggest machines in Almagest, but by building machines that could keep working where civilization had not yet caught up.

DOCUMENT TYPE: Canonical company history and ecosystem profile

CANON STATUS: Current master version

PRIMARY DIVISION: H-E-I Shipyards - Almagest Division

SCOPE: Pre-Almagest origins through the modern Almagest era

FOUNDATION AND PRE-ALMAGEST PROGRAMS

1. COMPANY IDENTITY

H-E-I stands for Helix Engineering & Integration.

H-E-I was never one of humanity's enormous colonial megacorporations. In the Solar System it was a comparatively modest engineering and systems-integration company: large enough to undertake serious aerospace and defense work, but nowhere near large enough to direct humanity's interstellar colonization effort itself.

That distinction is important.

H-E-I's importance did not come from possessing enormous fleets, controlling governments, or dominating the Bering Project.

It came from being very good at making complicated systems actually work together.

Before Almagest, H-E-I specialized in fields such as spacecraft integration, diagnostics, flight control, sensors, structural systems, redundant control architecture, support hardware, repairability, and the integration of equipment produced by different manufacturers into coherent working platforms.

Its engineering culture developed around a simple practical reality:

A system that performs extraordinarily well under perfect conditions but cannot be repaired or supported in the field is often less useful than a slightly less sophisticated system that continues functioning when everything goes wrong.

That philosophy would eventually become one of the defining principles of HEI's Almagest-era ships.

2. THE PRE-ALMAGEST PROGRAMS

HEI's transformation began shortly before humanity departed for Almagest.

By 2081, HEI had received work connected to what became the Compact Combat Vessel Program, or CCV Program.

The concept was ambitious but deliberately restrained in scale.

Instead of designing another large warship, the CCV program asked whether a relatively small vessel could perform patrol, escort, reconnaissance, inspection, search and rescue, remote-installation defense, limited cargo work, security operations, and combat while still being operated by a small crew and supported far from a major naval facility.

The principle that emerged from the program became central to HEI:

Remain useful when the mission changes.

The CCV work would eventually produce the Excalibur lineage.

At roughly the same time, HEI was also working on Advanced Materials.

One of the most important products of this research was the HEI Bi-Weave Hex Grid Graphite-Kevlar composite, a lightweight and flexible protective material intended to provide substantial ballistic resistance without the mass and rigidity of traditional armor systems.

The material became associated with HEI protective equipment and later spacesuit development. Early production was extremely limited, with only a few dozen initial examples available around the beginning of the Almagest era, but later versions became increasingly common throughout HEI equipment.

HEI also developed camouflage and surface-management systems associated with these suits, including SMP camouflage, which eventually evolved into the broader dual-environment camouflage philosophy used on modern HEI field equipment.

3. THE BERING PROJECT

Humanity's major interstellar colonization effort began in 2083.

The Bering Project would send colonists approximately 10,000 light-years from Earth to the Almagest system.

The journey would take nearly 10,000 years.

Most passengers would spend almost the entire voyage in cryogenic suspension.

There was no practical return journey.

H-E-I participated in the project, but it was not one of the primary organizations controlling it.

Its role was much closer to that of a specialized technical contractor.

HEI personnel, engineering knowledge, research programs, fabrication information, and technical specialists were carried aboard the expedition. Thousands of HEI personnel would ultimately remain in cryogenic storage after the colony arrived, giving the organization a reservoir of specialists who could be awakened as the colony's industrial requirements expanded.

Shortly before departure, HEI also received access to an AI research division tasked with continuing work on projects that already existed rather than inventing an entirely new technological civilization from nothing.

The Advanced Materials and Compact Combat Vessel programs were among the priority projects.

4. TEN THOUSAND YEARS OF ENGINEERING

While humanity slept, automated research did not simply stop.

The Almagest expedition's research systems spent thousands of years processing engineering models.

Millions of configurations could be simulated, rejected, revised, and refined before anyone had to spend real material building them.

Research extended across spacecraft hull architecture, propulsion integration, life support, manufacturing, industrial systems, materials science, spacesuit technology, and related engineering disciplines.

This did not mean colonists arrived to find ten thousand years of magical technological progress waiting for them.

Much of the work still had to be physically realized, tested, adapted to locally available materials, and manufactured using the colony's actual industrial capability.

HEI therefore arrived with something extremely valuable:

A vast body of engineering work that still needed engineers.

That distinction shaped the company's post-arrival rise.

ARRIVAL, REORGANIZATION, AND EARLY INDUSTRY

5. ARRIVAL IN ALMAGEST

The expedition eventually reached the Almagest system.

The system is centered on the star Almagest and also contains the brown dwarf Delfos.

The first major settlement world was Verdure, an unexpectedly habitable world possessing a breathable environment and an Earth-like biosphere.

Other established system locations include Palatine, the Viridian Halo, Kemik, Caligo, the Cryon Ring, and the outer ocean world Byblos, although not every body's exact role in HEI's early history has yet been equally developed.

The first colonists descended to Verdure and began the basic work necessary to rebuild civilization:

reactors were activated, shelters erected, machinery revived, mines established, habitats constructed, and permanent settlements gradually formed.

The early colony was anything but comfortable.

Ships were reused, repaired, modified, salvaged, and pressed into jobs they had never originally been intended to perform.

Permanent infrastructure was limited.

Long-distance support was difficult.

Manufacturing capacity was precious.

Under those circumstances, HEI's existing engineering culture suddenly became extremely valuable.

6. H-E-I REBORN

Following arrival, the company reorganized around its new environment.

The resulting organization became:

H-E-I Shipyards - Almagest Division

The Colonial Authority gave HEI resources and authorization to establish an independent orbital engineering and shipbuilding capability.

Initially, HEI was primarily doing what it had always done best:

repairing things.

Colony spacecraft required modification.

Cargo vessels had to be strengthened.

Frames had to be adapted for roles their original designers had never anticipated.

Control systems needed reconfiguration.

Industrial machinery required integration.

Local production methods needed to be standardized.

HEI's early Almagest success came from making whatever hardware humanity already possessed more useful, more maintainable, and better suited to frontier conditions.

The company did not arrive in Almagest as a major shipbuilder.

It became one because the colony needed one.

7. THE FIRST HEI FACILITIES

HEI's first dedicated installations were modest compared with what would eventually follow.

One early asteroid facility incorporated artificial gravity, stable oxygen production, reactor baseline power, solar arrays mounted on exposed structural trusses, storage, and docking capability.

A reinforced-glass recreation area helped make the facility livable rather than simply functional.

HEI's station philosophy was already visible:

build exactly as much infrastructure as necessary, expose what can safely remain accessible, armor or protect what matters, and make expansion possible.

8. YEAR TWO - FROM REPAIR YARD TO SHIPBUILDER

By 2 AE HEI Shipyards was undergoing a major transition.

The company expanded from repair, modification, and retrofit work into:

shipbuilding, manufacturing, and large-scale reconstruction.

The Colonial Authority provided additional resources, personnel, and manufacturing contracts as HEI demonstrated that it could produce dependable frontier hardware locally.

The early production sequence was:

Expedition Shuttle -> Featherfall Freighter -> Outlander Industrial Platform -> Borehole Miner

The Excalibur project continued alongside this work as a much more ambitious military and expeditionary program.

These early civilian ships became disproportionately important to the colony.

They moved personnel.

They moved cargo.

They moved resources.

They supported construction.

They connected settlements.

They made expansion possible before large permanent infrastructure existed everywhere humanity wanted to go.

This was the period when HEI stopped merely supporting Almagest's industrial network and began becoming part of the network itself.

THE EARLY HEI CIVILIAN FLEET

9. THE EXPEDITION SHUTTLE

The Expedition Shuttle was the first major HEI-produced Almagest spacecraft to come off the line.

It remained recognizably a shuttle, but had significantly greater endurance and capability than most small craft operating in the early colony.

Its basic purpose was straightforward:

move personnel and equipment across distances that ordinary utility craft struggled to cover reliably.

It became useful for station servicing, remote operations, local transport, exploration support, and ship-to-surface or ship-to-installation movement.

Later shuttles also became part of HEI's larger ship ecosystem.

The Excalibur maintains an internal hangar specifically capable of carrying an HEI shuttle, while the modern Outlander includes external docking areas that can support shuttle operations.

10. FEATHER FALL

The HEI Feather Fall / Featherfall Freighter followed the Shuttle.

Its defining purpose is logistics.

Where the Excalibur moves crews and mission capability, the Feather Fall moves material.

It became one of the early logistical backbones of the colony, carrying components, supplies, construction material, resources, and industrial cargo between settlements and remote operations.

Earlier HEI material also frames the Feather Fall as a planetary cargo transport, emphasizing its importance in moving heavy logistical loads into areas where permanent transportation infrastructure did not yet exist.

In the modern fleet, Feather Falls remain part of the distributed logistics system.

The new Outlander specifically incorporates external docking/landing positions where Feather Falls can transfer supplies directly to the larger industrial vessel.

The exact modern technical specification of the Feather Fall remains less developed than the Excalibur, Outlander, Borehole, or Sojourner.

11. THE ORIGINAL OUTLANDER

The Outlander emerged as HEI's larger frontier industrial and logistics platform.

The original vessel was intentionally practical.

It was relatively simple.

Easy to build.

Easy to repair.

Not particularly graceful.

And capable of functioning for long periods away from developed infrastructure.

Its primary propulsion still required fuel, but ion maneuvering systems and solar generation provided the ship with a degree of long-duration self-sufficiency even when the main drive could not be operated indefinitely.

The original Outlander served as a cargo carrier and industrial-support platform, but its most important relationship was with the Borehole.

The two were designed together.

The Borehole mined.

The Outlander sustained the mining operation.

The Borehole could be carried between the Outlander's forward structures between extraction missions.

The original platform could also perform planetary operations, although very heavy cargo loads significantly limited its gravity capability.

Outlander became a classic example of early HEI thinking:

not exceptional at one job, but useful in situations where a more specialized vessel would become dependent on infrastructure that did not exist.

12. THE BOREHOLE

The Borehole was HEI's dedicated mobile resource-extraction platform.

Unlike a general-purpose industrial ship with mining tools added afterward, the Borehole was designed around its drill.

The drill was not equipment carried by the spacecraft.

The spacecraft existed to support the drill.

This gave the class its defining central structure and made the Borehole one of HEI's most recognizable industrial ships.

Successive generations increased capability without abandoning that basic architecture.

The later Borehole Mk 4 brought increased thrust, an improved drill, and lightweight habitation, while remaining primarily a space-oriented extraction vessel.

Over its long operational life, the Borehole became one of HEI's most trusted and cherished industrial designs.

THE EXCALIBUR PROGRAM

13. THE COMPACT COMBAT VESSEL BECOMES EXCALIBUR

Meanwhile, HEI's old Compact Combat Vessel work had continued to evolve.

The early CCV concept was intended to perform many different duties with a small crew and relatively small hull.

As Almagest expanded, its role grew.

Patrol became long-range patrol.

Reconnaissance became exploration.

Escort operations pushed farther from support.

Search-and-rescue demanded longer endurance.

Expeditionary operations increasingly required vehicles, supplies, landing capability, and onboard accommodation.

The result became what HEI eventually termed the Star Chaser concept.

A Star Chaser was not simply supposed to travel far.

It was supposed to arrive far away carrying enough capability to do something useful when it got there.

14. EXCALIBUR MOD 6

The recognizable Excalibur lineage begins with Mod 6.

The ship was approximately:

73 m long x 35 m wide x 15 m tall.

It was ambitious, somewhat overbuilt, and extremely dense.

Most importantly, Mod 6 established the weapon that would become inseparable from the Excalibur name:

XR-9 "Godspear"

The XR-9 was integrated as a spinal railgun rather than simply fitted to the ship externally.

The Excalibur's structure became part of the weapon system.

That allowed a relatively compact corvette to threaten vessels significantly larger than itself.

HEI also became known for the PDX-44 automated point-defense cannon, another technology strongly associated with the Excalibur program.

The combination of precision heavy kinetic firepower and automated defensive coverage helped transform HEI from a respected frontier integrator into a legitimate military ship and weapons developer.

H-E-I remained the sole producer of the Excalibur lineage.

15. MOD 6 THROUGH MK 12

The original hull was revised repeatedly.

From Mod 6 through Mk 12, HEI altered propulsion, armor, compartmentalization, engineering access, life support, cargo arrangements, power architecture, landing capability, and weapon integration.

The Excalibur gradually changed from a compact combat ship into a true long-range expeditionary corvette.

Mk 11 represented the mature form of the original design.

It incorporated the lessons of years of modification and became closely associated with improved HEI protective equipment and the growing integration of HEI's advanced materials.

Mk 12 represented the practical end of the old hull.

HEI could keep modifying it.

But the company was increasingly designing around decisions that had been made much earlier in the program.

So it stopped.

16. 1-M

MODEL: Excalibur Class 1-M Starchaser

FIRST REVISION: R-1.0

DIMENSIONS: 79.5 m x 45 m x 17.5 m

TYPICAL CREW: 6-8 personnel

The proposed next major modification became something much larger.

Originally treated as the next step after Mk 12, the project was eventually taken back to a clean sheet.

After roughly 18 months of development, the new frame became:

HEI Excalibur Class 1-M Starchaser

The designation 1-M identifies the model/design.

The revision identifier is placed at the end.

The first production-standard version therefore became:

( H-E-I ) Excalibur Class 1-M Starchaser R-1.0

The clean-sheet ship measured approximately:

79.5 m x 45 m x 17.5 m

with a typical crew of:

6-8 personnel.

It retained everything fundamental to Excalibur:

the XR-9, strong armor, small crew, substantial power, cargo, expeditionary capability, a shuttle hangar, atmospheric operation, and the ability to operate independently for long periods.

17. NOSTROMO

The Nostromo exists in the current broader HEI/Almagest fleet canon as a major line warship and capital-combat platform.

Its construction began early and was accelerated following the Excalibur's first-contact incident.

It became one of humanity's earliest major capital responses to the possibility of large-scale hostile contact.

Its scale has generally been placed in the roughly 200-300 meter range, with later story material placing it around the upper end of that range.

It is heavily armed, supports major sensor and command capability, and includes a dedicated hangar capable of carrying an Excalibur.

The Nostromo is also associated with higher-level operational command away from the main HEI facilities.

Some older weapon descriptions for the Nostromo differ - particularly between a six-forward-railgun arrangement and later multi-turret concepts - so its exact final weapon battery has not been normalized as tightly as the Excalibur's.

It remains part of the current fleet canon, but its exact relationship to HEI manufacturing is less completely locked than the core HEI-designed vessels.

THE HEI MODERNIZATION ERA

18. THE MODERNIZATION ERA

Years of Excalibur development eventually began influencing the rest of HEI.

By this point the company possessed much greater industrial capability than the organization that had first arrived in Almagest.

But many older ships were still products of early colonial necessity.

The question became:

What happens when HEI applies everything it has learned to the ships that built the frontier?

That began a broader modernization program.

The Borehole was reconsidered.

The Outlander was almost completely rebuilt.

The Sojourner was designed as an entirely new civilian platform.

And eventually the Excalibur itself returned to the modernization docket.

The philosophy was consistent across all of them:

  • Do not replace something merely because it is old.
  • Keep what works.
  • Strengthen what fails.
  • Simplify what became unnecessarily complicated.
  • Improve maintainability.
  • Increase range.
  • Support the crew properly.
  • Use modularity where permanent specialization wastes space.

19. THE MODERN BOREHOLE

CORE DRILL: Retained almost unchanged

PROPULSION: Approx. 5x previous thrust

PASSIVE POWER: 8 small solar panels

CREW: 2 workers with full amenities

The next-generation Borehole received one of the most significant upgrades in its history.

HEI deliberately retained the ship's proven central drill almost unchanged.

Everything around it was reconsidered.

The new frame was strengthened.

The overall architecture was simplified.

Fuel reserves increased.

Oxygen capacity increased.

And propulsion improved dramatically.

The new Borehole produces approximately:

MODERN BOREHOLE: approximately 5x the thrust of the previous generation

This fundamentally changes how quickly it can deploy, relocate between deposits, and return to its support vessel.

Eight small solar panels are angled around the hull, giving the ship passive power generation across a wider range of orientations during long-duration operations.

The largest change is habitability.

The new Borehole is fully capable of supporting:

2 workers

in a proper crew cabin with full amenities.

The Borehole is therefore no longer merely a machine that crews occupy for a short working shift.

It is a genuine crewed frontier mining vessel capable of sustained independent operations.

20. THE MODERN OUTLANDER

ROLE: Long-range mobile industrial node

PROPULSION: Approx. 2x previous thrust

RANGE: Approx. 2x previous range

BOREHOLE CARRIAGE: Between forward arms

The modern Outlander was redesigned at much larger scale than the Borehole.

Like the old pair, the new Outlander and Borehole were designed together.

The Borehole remains physically carried between the Outlander's forward arms between mining operations.

But the new Outlander is far more than a mining tender.

It is now a long-range:

industrial platform, cargo vessel, logistics ship, recovery platform, support ship, and mobile production center.

Its onboard industrial suite is capable of producing components at scale, allowing an Outlander to support construction, repair, resupply, maintenance, and remote industrial operations without constantly returning to fixed infrastructure.

Compared with the old ship, the modern Outlander has approximately:

2x the thrust

and

2x the range

It retains operation both inside and outside gravity.

Several external landing/docking areas support Feather Fall freighters, shuttles, and other small utility craft.

Feather Falls can exchange cargo directly with the Outlander.

Shuttles can dock.

The Borehole can conduct extraction.

The Outlander can manufacture, store, repair, support, and redistribute.

The modern Outlander therefore functions as a mobile industrial node.

It is intentionally not a dedicated shipbuilding vessel with a giant integrated welding system.

HEI's preference is broader utility.

A small welder craft may be carried when required.

21. SOJOURNER

The HEI Sojourner-class was created during the same modernization period.

Its purpose was completely different.

The growing civilian population of Almagest needed a ship designed not for large industry or military operations, but for an individual person trying to build a life on the frontier.

Concept work began several years into the broader modernization period, while major Excalibur refits were also reshaping HEI design philosophy.

The design requirement was deliberately straightforward:

Tough. Reliable. Useful. Simple to build.

The Sojourner was intended for settlers, prospectors, contractors, independent engineers, and other civilian operators who could not assume that a station or support ship would always be nearby.

It includes:

a survival kit, an O2/H2 generator, four small hydrogen tanks, two small cargo containers, four medium rear main thrusters, two Gatling guns, and two rocket launchers.

The weapons are primarily defensive.

The Sojourner is not a fighter.

Its armament exists because civilian ships operating beyond regular security coverage may occasionally have to protect themselves long enough to escape.

The craft is approximately 17 m long, 13 m wide, and 5 m tall based on its current visual model, with each top cockpit glass panel providing a 2.5 m scale reference.

It also incorporates solar capability and atmospheric/planetary utility.

The Sojourner is deliberately not exceptional at any one job.

Its value comes from the opposite idea:

It should still be useful when there is no other ship available.

22. EXCALIBUR REVISION 2

MODEL: Excalibur Class 1-M

REVISION: R-2.0

THEMES: Modularity, habitability, automation, survivability, extended flexibility

The same modernization thinking eventually returned to the Excalibur.

The current major update is:

( H-E-I ) Excalibur Class 1-M Starchaser R-2.0

The 1-M remains the model designation.

R-2.0 is the revision identifier and always appears at the end.

R-2.0 is not a new clean-sheet Excalibur.

It is the modernization of the existing 1-M.

Its central themes are:

modularity, habitability, automation, survivability, and extended operational flexibility.

23. EXCALIBUR R-2.0 MISSION PYLONS

The defining new capability is a system of:

7 modular external mission pylons

These allow mission-specific equipment to be carried outside the hull.

Possible loads include vehicles, external cargo, deployables, fuel pods, small habitation modules, specialist equipment, and weapons.

This preserves the internal hangar for larger protected cargo or the standard HEI shuttle.

The philosophical change is significant.

Earlier Excaliburs were mostly configured by deciding what could fit inside them.

R-2.0 increasingly works as a strong core platform onto which the mission is attached.

24. R-2.0 WEAPONS

The XR-9 Godspear remains the main offensive weapon.

The earlier six-PDC defensive network has been expanded through the pylon structure.

Four additional PDCs can be mounted on the horizontal pylon assembly, using its upper and lower surfaces.

The current defensive total is therefore:

10 PDCs

Revision 2 also permits a dedicated heavy-strike configuration carrying:

4 anti-capital torpedoes

on the external pylons.

These torpedoes are not permanent baseline armament.

They are a mission-specific strike package.

25. EXCALIBUR PROPULSION

The baseline R-2.0 propulsion configuration currently includes:

  • 2 x 7.5 m XL rear hydrogen thrusters
  • 36 large vertical/lift thrusters
  • 16 lateral thrusters
  • 6 additional upward/directional thrusters
  • 2 forward braking thrusters

Two separate external propulsion packages exist.

The ALK-4 is a hydrogen nacelle package.

It uses four nacelles, each carrying three medium hydrogen thrusters:

12 medium hydrogen thrusters total

The ETIK-2, or Extended Thrust Integration Kit, is a separate ion-thruster augmentation system.

Its exact canonical thruster count has not yet been fixed.

The purpose of both systems is to allow propulsion capability to scale with mission needs, particularly when the Excalibur is carrying substantial external payload.

26. EXCALIBUR REACTOR CITADEL

R-2.0 also fundamentally revises the central power installation.

The current configuration uses:

4 main reactors

Each reactor sits inside an individually reinforced, heavily armored housing within the already protected reactor citadel.

This replaces the older arrangement built around a larger number of small reactors.

The updated citadel reflects modern HEI design:

reduce unnecessary complexity, package systems more intelligently, and protect the components whose loss would actually kill the ship.

27. EXCALIBUR CREW AND HABITABILITY

R-2.0 also reflects HEI's increasing recognition that crew endurance is part of ship endurance.

The commons is expanded.

The kitchen becomes a significantly larger, fully functional galley.

The CIC is expanded.

A new detailed status/readout system is placed in the hallway near the command area.

The basic command philosophy remains unchanged:

an exposed navigation bridge for normal operation and visibility,

paired with an armored Combat Information Center deeper within the ship for combat operations.

28. EXCALIBUR HANGAR AND LANDING SYSTEM

The hangar remains central to the Starchaser concept.

R-2.0 includes improved armored clamps protecting the hangar hinge assemblies.

The landing gear also undergoes a major redesign.

Earlier Excaliburs required the landing gear to be manually deployed.

R-2.0 introduces automatic deployment.

The gear now retracts tightly into armored housings, leaving the underside significantly more flush and aerodynamically clean.

29. CURRENT EXCALIBUR MASS

The current R-2.0 baseline mass is:

R-2.0 BASELINE MASS: 5.5 million kilograms without external propulsion packages installed

without external propulsion packages installed.

Mission-loaded mass can vary dramatically depending on pylons, fuel pods, vehicles, cargo, torpedoes, habitat modules, and propulsion kits.

That variability is now intentional.

There is increasingly no single meaningful "fully loaded Excalibur."

There is the core Excalibur, and then there is the configuration chosen for the mission.

CURRENT FLEET, VEHICLES, INFRASTRUCTURE, AND EQUIPMENT

30. THE CURRENT HEI CIVILIAN/INDUSTRIAL FLEET

SHUTTLE: Personnel / local utility

SOJOURNER: Independent frontier craft

FEATHER FALL: Cargo / logistics

BOREHOLE: Resource extraction

OUTLANDER: Mobile industry / support

EXCALIBUR: Expeditionary reach / security

NOSTROMO: Capital-combat layer

The present civilian side of HEI is centered around a complementary family of vessels.

The Shuttle handles personnel and local utility movement.

The Sojourner provides an individual colonist with a small self-sufficient frontier craft.

The Feather Fall moves cargo and material.

The Borehole extracts resources.

The Outlander supports mining, industrial production, logistics, salvage, recovery, and remote operations.

The Excalibur carries a small crew and whatever mission capability is required when the mission may involve exploration, security, combat, emergency response, vehicle deployment, or operating somewhere the rest of the fleet cannot yet safely work.

The Nostromo occupies the heavy capital-combat layer of the broader fleet.

31. GROUND VEHICLE PROGRAM

HEI also maintains a growing vehicle family.

The Light Recon / Light Offroad Vehicle is a high-clearance, trophy-truck-inspired rover built for long-range, high-speed travel over rough planetary terrain.

It includes cargo capability and is sized specifically to fit within the Excalibur's hangar.

The LMV - Light Multipurpose Vehicle is a modular utility platform.

Current established configurations include the LMV Base, LMV Light Cargo, LMV Personnel Transport, and LMV Refueling Rig.

The Refueling Rig includes a trailer/pad arrangement large enough to service a shuttle.

The platform has also been considered for a mining variant, with a dedicated small mining shuttle intended to operate from the refueling system.

The entire vehicle family reflects the same HEI philosophy as the ships:

use common architecture, then adapt it to the mission.

32. HEI INFRASTRUCTURE

Current HEI infrastructure includes the:

  • ( H-E-I ) Production Outpost
  • ( H-E-I ) Light Landing Pad / Refueling Depot
  • ( H-E-I ) All In One Asteroid Base (S)
  • ( H-E-I ) Light Landing Pad
  • ( H-E-I ) HAB Module XR-H1
  • HAB Solar Cell
  • HAB Addon SOL-1
  • HAB Addon PRD-1/PW
  • HAB Addon C-01

The XR-H1 is a compact deployable habitation system suitable for transport by vessels such as the Excalibur.

A small standardized asteroid outpost configuration has been designed around enough manufacturing, fuel processing, docking, and basic support capability to sustain a modest local fleet.

One established capacity concept supports approximately:

2 Feather Falls, 1 Outlander or Starchaser-sized vessel, 2 Boreholes, and 4 shuttles.

HEI also uses deployable outposts that can be transported by a Starchaser or another suitable carrier.

Fuel depots and asteroid-mounted defensive turret platforms have also been under development.

Support systems include the Excalibur Planetary Landing Pod and the shuttle-compatible LMV refueling trailer/pad.

Older Communication Outpost and Survival Shelter designs are considered legacy/non-current rather than part of the active infrastructure lineup.

33. HEI PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT

HEI's spacesuit and protective-equipment philosophy closely mirrors its spacecraft engineering.

The common principles are:

modularity, durability, serviceability, EVA capability, and shared hardware wherever practical.

Common systems include magnetic boots, maneuvering thrusters, modular backpack interfaces, HUD and sensor equipment, vacuum protection, and standardized tool mounting.

HEI's modern suit visual identity uses combinations of olive or military green, dark gray, black, white visibility markings, and the company's orange accents.

The current HEI Commander baseline uses a Multicam-derived dual-environment pattern, orange HEI identification bands, a clean F-16-style orange/gold tinted visor, Helix shoulder insignia, gray/multicam backpack, and blue electronic/status elements.

Earlier skull visor graphics and the TAPS-style chest rig are not part of the current canonical Commander configuration.

The wider suit family includes general operations, industrial workforce, environmental-specialist, and advanced/support equipment.

Established role concepts include standard personnel, logistics handlers, pilots, shipyard workers, construction/rigger personnel, technicians, mining personnel, salvage workers, surveyors, science personnel, medical/rescue personnel, and dedicated Hazard Operations equipment for high-risk reactor, radiation, refinery, chemical, or damaged-ship environments.

ENGINEERING PHILOSOPHY AND COMPANY LEGACY

34. THE MODERN HEI ENGINEERING PHILOSOPHY

By the modern era, HEI's design culture can be reduced to several recurring ideas.

Preserve proven systems.

The modern Borehole kept the drill.

Rebuild the weak structure around them.

The Borehole frame changed dramatically.

Turn dependency into mobility.

The Outlander carries industrial capability into the frontier.

Do not waste protected internal volume.

Excalibur R-2.0 moves mission loads onto external pylons.

Support the people operating the machine.

The modern Borehole gains real crew accommodation; the Excalibur gains better commons, kitchen, CIC, and information access.

Automate repetitive workload when the automation can be trusted.

Excalibur's landing gear becomes automatic.

Design for repair instead of assuming replacement.

Do not specialize a ship so completely that one change of mission makes it useless.

That last principle is the oldest of all.

It traces directly back to the CCV program:

Remain useful when the mission changes.

35. WHAT HEI BECAME

H-E-I did not arrive in Almagest as the organization capable of building all of this.

That is the central point of its history.

It arrived as a comparatively small engineering contractor.

Humanity's new civilization lacked mature infrastructure.

So HEI repaired ships.

Then it modified them.

Then it manufactured components.

Then it built shuttles.

Then freighters.

Then industrial ships.

Then miners.

Then increasingly advanced military spacecraft.

Eventually it built the infrastructure that allowed those ships to operate even farther from established settlements.

Its rise was not based on suddenly becoming a gigantic corporation.

It was based on being useful at exactly the moment usefulness mattered most.

The colony needed equipment that was repairable.

HEI built it.

It needed ships that could survive beyond support networks.

HEI built them.

It needed mobile industry.

HEI built it.

It needed a corvette capable of going first into unknown territory.

HEI built the Excalibur.

And as Almagest expanded, those individual solutions gradually became an integrated ecosystem.

MASTER PRINCIPLE

36. HEI IN ONE SENTENCE

If the entire company history had to be reduced to one principle, it would be this:

Helix Engineering & Integration became indispensable not by building the biggest machines in Almagest, but by building machines that could keep working where civilization had not yet caught up.

That is what connects the first repairs after arrival, the Expedition Shuttle, Feather Fall, Borehole, Outlander, Sojourner, Excalibur, HEI's outposts, its suits, and the current modernization era.

They are all different answers to the same problem:

How do you keep people operating when the frontier is larger than the infrastructure supporting them?

H-E-I's answer has consistently been:

build something tough, integrate it properly, make it repairable, give it enough independence to survive, and make sure it can still do something useful when the original plan stops working.
